Demographic changes and the shrinking working-age population will heighten pressure on social security sys- tems and increase the need for younger workers to fill gaps.

...

Nursing professionals moved up from the fifth most widespread shortage occupation in 2023 to the second in 2024. The OECD (2022, 2024a) high- lights that the pandemic intensified worker shortages, as burnout and deteriorating working conditions prompted many professionals to leave the healthcare sector. The resulting staff deficits have created a vicious cycle, where fewer workers lead to increased workloads and further res- ignations. This persistent trend suggests that shortages in healthcare are structural rather than transient, compound- ed by the ageing population and the long training require- ments for medical professions.
Labour shortages in the construction sector have also intensified since the COVID-19 pandemic, with shortages now three times higher than they were a decade ago (Eu- ropean Commission, 2023a). The demand for skilled trades such as welders and flame cutters (23 countries report shortages, 32 % of which are high severity), plumbers and pipe fitters (21 countries report shortages, 29 % of which are high severity) and building and related electricians (22 countries report shortages, 27 % of which are high severi- ty) has surged due to major infrastructure investments and green transition policies.
The hospitality sector continues to struggle with shortag- es of cooks (22 countries report shortages, 18 % of which are high severity), chefs (17 countries report shortages, 18 % of which are high severity) and waiters (18 coun- tries report shortages, 39 % of which are high severity), as the post-pandemic recovery led to a rapid rebound in demand that outpaced the labour supply (OECD, 2022, 2024a).

## EURES 2024: construction labour shortages in the countries you listed

**Construction-related occupations were reported as shortages in all eight countries—but not uniformly across every construction job.** The clearest country-level summary in EURES is for the broader occupation group **“Building and related trades workers, excluding electricians.”**

| Country | EURES 2024 construction-related signal |
|---|---|
| **Portugal** | Building and related trades workers were among the occupation groups most often reported in shortage. Portugal also reported many occupations as both shortage and surplus, which can reflect regional or other differences. ([eures.europa.eu](https://eures.europa.eu/living-and-working/labour-market-information/labour-market-information-portugal_en?prefLang=nl&utm_source=openai)) |
| **Spain** | Construction labour shortages were reported for some occupations, but Spain also had many surplus occupations overall. So the picture is mixed, not a general shortage across construction. ([eures.europa.eu](https://eures.europa.eu/living-and-working/labour-market-information/labour-market-information-spain_en?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Germany** | Building and related trades workers were among the occupation groups with the highest occurrence of shortages. ([eures.europa.eu](https://eures.europa.eu/living-and-working/labour-market-information/labour-market-information-germany_en?utm_source=openai)) |
| **France** | Building and related trades workers were among the occupation groups with the highest occurrence of shortages. ([eures.europa.eu](https://eures.europa.eu/living-and-working/labour-market-information/labour-market-information-france_en?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Italy** | The European Labour Authority lists Italy among the countries reporting the greatest numbers of shortage occupations overall; that does **not** by itself establish a shortage in every construction occupation. ([ela.europa.eu](https://www.ela.europa.eu/en/news/gaps-european-labour-market-2024-continue-increase)) |
| **Croatia** | Building and related trades workers were among the occupation groups with the highest occurrence of shortages. ([eures.europa.eu](https://eures.europa.eu/living-and-working/labour-market-information/labour-market-information-croatia_en?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Cyprus** | The report’s country-level summary indicates a comparatively balanced overall mix of shortages and surpluses; that should not be read as proof that construction had no shortages. ([ela.europa.eu](https://www.ela.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2025-06/EURES_Report_on_labour_shortages_and_surpluses_2024.pdf)) |
| **Netherlands** | The report describes the Netherlands as having many shortage occupations relative to few surpluses overall, but that is not a construction-only finding. ([ela.europa.eu](https://www.ela.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2025-06/EURES_Report_on_labour_shortages_and_surpluses_2024.pdf)) |

**Bottom line:** The strongest direct construction-group evidence among your list is for **Germany, France, Croatia, and Portugal**. For Spain, Italy, Cyprus, and the Netherlands, the cited country summaries do not support a simple “construction shortage” label across the sector.

**Important caveat:** EURES’ 2024 report compiles national submissions, and countries use different data sources and methods. It identifies shortages by occupation, not as one comparable construction-sector shortage rate. ([eures.europa.eu](https://eures.europa.eu/living-and-working/labour-shortages-and-surpluses-europe_en))

Tourism statistics at regional level

Statistics Explained

Source : Statistics Explained (ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statisticsexplained/) - 23/10/2026 1
Data extracted in March and April 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 This article forms part of the Eurostat regional yearbook – 2026 , an annual flagship publication . It provides a detailed picture relating to a broad range of statistical topics across the regions of the EU , EFTA and candidate countries. A short reading guide is provided in the introductory chapter, including an explanation of how to interpret the maps.

Highlights

In August 2024, 494.7 million nights were spent in EU tourist accommodation, compared with fewer than 200 million per month from January to April, November and December.
In 2024, Mallorca recorded 55.3 million nights spent in tourist accommodation, the highest regional value across the EU; Roma, Paris and Barcelona each registered more than 40.0 million nights.

...

Tourism statistics are traditionally collected from suppliers of tourism services through surveys of tourist accommodation establishments or from administrative data. These establishments include all types of accommodation which provide, as a paid service, accommodation for tourists. They are defined according to the activity classification NACE and include:
• hotels and similar establishments (NACE Group 55.1)
• holiday and other short-stay accommodation (NACE Group 55.2)
• camping grounds, recreational vehicle parks and trailer parks (NACE Group 55.3) .
The number of nights spent in tourist accommodation reflects both the length of stay and the number of tourists and is considered a key indicator for examining tourism developments, even though it does not cover stays in non-rented accommodation or same-day visits (without an overnight stay).
The statistics presented in this section generally refer to 2024.

...

Looking in more detail at each month in 2024, the following NUTS level 2 regions recorded the highest numbers of nights spent in tourist accommodation by domestic and international tourists combined:
• January – Canarias (Spain), Ile-de-France and Rhône-Alpes (both France)
• February – Canarias, Rhône-Alpes and Tirol (Austria)
• March – Canarias, Ile-de-France and Andalucía (Spain)
• April – Canarias, Ile-de-France and Andalucía
• May – Illes Balears, Cataluña (both Spain) and Ile-de-France
• June – Jadranska Hrvatska (Croatia), Illes Balears and Cataluña
• July – Jadranska Hrvatska, Cataluña and Veneto (Italy)
• August – Jadranska Hrvatska, Cataluña and Veneto
• September – Illes Balears, Jadranska Hrvatska and Cataluña
• October – Canarias, Illes Balears and Ile-de-France
• November – Canarias, Ile-de-France and Andalucía

...

Jadranska Hrvatska on the Croatian Adriatic coastline recorded the highest number of nights spent by international tourists in the height of summer 2024
Turning to the most frequented NUTS level 2 regions among international tourists, Canarias in Spain recorded the highest number of nights spent in January to April 2024 and again in October to December 2024, reflecting its year-round appeal and relatively stable temperatures. During these months, the number of nights spent by international tourists ranged between 6.8 million and 8.1 million.
The Spanish island region of Illes Balears recorded the highest number of nights spent by international tourists in May 2024, with visitors to islands such as Mallorca and Ibiza benefitting from the favourable spring climate before the peak summer influx of tourists.
```

EU tourism tops 3 billion nights in 2024 after strong Q4

man holding luggage and hand in hotel room
© Davizro Photography/Shutterstock.com
2024 was the best tourism year on record for the EU , with the total number of nights spent at tourist accommodation establishments exceeding 3 billion. This reflects a 2.2% increase compared with 2023 (+65.4 million nights), following a final boost in the last quarter of the year.
Data show a substantial increase of 67.2 million nights spent by international guests (+4.9%) in 2024, while nights spent by domestic guests slightly decreased (-0.1%; -1.8 million).
Spain (500 million), Italy (458 million), France (451 million) and Germany (441 million) registered the highest number of nights spent at tourist accommodation establishments, representing 61.6% of the total nights spent in the EU. Robust Q4 2024: tourism nights up in almost all EU countries

The last quarter of 2024 was responsible for the soaring yearly results, with a 5.1% increase in the total nights spent in the EU compared with Q4 2023.
Tourism nights increased in all EU countries in Q4 2024 compared with the same quarter of 2023, except in Ireland where it decreased slightly (-1.8%). Among the other EU countries, the highest quarterly increases were registered in Malta (+16.5%), Latvia (+12.5%), Italy (+11.1%) and Croatia (+10.2%).

The number of nights spent by foreign tourists increased more significantly (+57.6%) than domestic tourists (+26.3%) from the base year 2010 (see Figure 4).
Figure 4
In 2024, Spain was the most visited tourism destination in the EU for international tourists (people travelling outside their country), with 322 million nights spent in tourist accommodation establishments, or 22.2% of the EU total (see Figure 5 and Figure 6). In 2024, the top 5 NUTS 3 regions in the EU were Mallorca, Roma, Barcelona, Tenerife and Venezia.

* Excel Tourism statistics: tables

Data sources

Tourism, in a statistical context, refers to the activity of visitors taking a trip to a destination outside their usual environment, for less than a year. It can be for any main purpose, including business, leisure or other personal reasons other than to be employed by a resident person, household or enterprise in the place visited.
In July 2011, the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union adopted Regulation (EU) No 692/2011 concerning European statistics on tourism and repealing Council Directive 95/57/EC ; requiring EU Member States to provide a regular set of comparable tourism statistics.
Tourism statistics in the EU consist of 2 main components: on the one hand, statistics relating to capacity and occupancy of collective tourist accommodation; on the other, statistics relating to tourism demand.

...

In addition, statistics on the use of bedrooms and bed places ( occupancy rates ) are compiled. From the reference year 2018 onwards, Eurostat also publishes, as separate series, data on occupancy of short-term rentals booked via Airbnb, Booking or Expedia Group.
Statistics on tourism demand are collected in relation to the number of tourism trips made (and the number of nights spent on those trips), separated by:
* destination country;
* purpose;
* length of stay;
* accommodation type;
* departure month;
* transport mode;
* expenditure.
The data are also analysed by the socio-demographic characteristics of the tourist:
* sex;
* age group;
* educational attainment level (optional);
* household income (optional);
* activity status (optional).

# Tourism statistics at regional level

[Print this page pdf](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/SEPDF/cache/1945.pdf?v=4412275758827272)

[Skip to the content](#se-top-of-article)

Data extracted in March and April 2026

Planned article update: September 2027

This article forms part of the *[Eurostat regional yearbook – 2026](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Eurostat_regional_yearbook)*, an annual [flagship publication](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/main/publications/flagship-publications). It provides a detailed picture relating to a broad range of statistical topics across the regions of the [EU](/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:EU "Glossary:EU"), [EFTA](/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA) "Glossary:European Free Trade Association (EFTA)") and [candidate](/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Candidate_countries "Glossary:Candidate countries") countries. A [short reading guide](/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Regional_yearbook_introduction#A_short_reading_guide "Regional yearbook introduction") is provided in the introductory chapter, including an explanation of how to interpret the maps.

## Highlights

In August 2024, 494.7 million nights were spent in EU tourist accommodation, compared with fewer than 200 million per month from January to April, November and December.

In 2024, Mallorca recorded 55.3 million nights spent in tourist accommodation, the highest regional value across the EU; Roma, Paris and Barcelona each registered more than 40.0 million nights.

[![An infographic showing EU regions with the highest number of nights spent in tourist accommodation. Data are presented for the ten regions with the highest number of nights spent in 2024. Data are shown in millions of nights for NUTS level 3 regions in the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.](/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/6/64/RYB-Infographics-CH10_RYB2026.png/700px-RYB-Infographics-CH10_RYB2026.png)](/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:RYB-Infographics-CH10_RYB2026.png)

**Source:* Eurostat ([tour_occ_nin3](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/783347bd-f2b9-4984-8f11-014f806e273a?lang=en))*

With diverse landscapes, rich cultural heritage and world-class attractions, the EU is a leading tourist destination. Indeed, [tourism](/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Tourism "Glossary:Tourism") plays a key role in the EU economy, contributing significantly to economic growth, employment and regional development. It can potentially support regional economies, particularly in [coastal](/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Coastal_region "Glossary:Coastal region"), [mountain](/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Mountain_region "Glossary:Mountain region") or [outermost regions](https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/policy/themes/outermost-regions_en), while also fostering cross-border connections. Jobs created or maintained by tourism can help counteract industrial or rural decline by sustaining local services and infrastructure that might otherwise decline.

Tourism can have negative consequences or externalities. It presents economic challenges, such as seasonal employment fluctuations or excessive demand during peak seasons, placing a strain on local infrastructure and/or acting as a nuisance for local communities. Tourism also has an environmental impact: locally through noise, pollution, waste generation, wastewater discharge and habitat loss, and globally through transport emissions. Understanding regional tourism patterns helps policymakers develop strategies for sustainable growth, balancing economic benefits with social and environmental impacts.

The infographic above provides information on the EU regions with the highest numbers of [nights spent](/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Nights_spent "Glossary:Nights spent") in [tourist accommodation](/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Tourist_accommodation_establishment "Glossary:Tourist accommodation establishment") during 2024. The list includes popular destinations for:

- beach holidays, such as Mallorca, Tenerife, Alicante/Alacant or Málaga in Spain
- city destinations, such as Barcelona or Venezia, as well as the Italian, French and Spanish capital regions of Roma, Paris and Madrid
- mountain destinations, such as Bolzano-Bozen in northern Italy.

## Number of nights spent in tourist accommodation

**More about the data: tourism statistics**

Tourism, in a statistical context, refers to the activity of people taking a trip to a destination outside their usual environment, for less than a year. This definition is wider than the common everyday definition, insofar as it encompasses not only private leisure trips but also visits to family and friends, as well as business trips. Visitors include tourists (who are visitors with at least 1 overnight stay – as presented in this chapter) and same-day visitors.

Tourism statistics are traditionally collected from suppliers of tourism services through surveys of tourist accommodation establishments or from administrative data. These establishments include all types of accommodation which provide, as a paid service, accommodation for tourists. They are defined according to the activity classification [NACE](/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE) "Glossary:Statistical classification of economic activities in the European Community (NACE)") and include:

- [hotels and similar establishments (NACE Group 55.1)](/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Hotels_and_similar_accommodation "Glossary:Hotels and similar accommodation")
- [holiday and other short-stay accommodation (NACE Group 55.2)](/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Holiday_and_other_short-stay_accommodation "Glossary:Holiday and other short-stay accommodation")
- [camping grounds, recreational vehicle parks and trailer parks (NACE Group 55.3)](/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Camping_grounds,_recreational_vehicle_parks_and_trailer_parks "Glossary:Camping grounds, recreational vehicle parks and trailer parks").

The number of nights spent in tourist accommodation reflects both the length of stay and the number of tourists and is considered a key indicator for examining tourism developments, even though it does not cover stays in non-rented accommodation or same-day visits (without an overnight stay).

The statistics presented in this section generally refer to 2024. They are typically shown for NUTS level 3 regions. However, for Belgium, the breakdown between domestic and international tourists is available only at NUTS level 2. For Türkiye, data are available only at NUTS level 2 for the total, domestic and international tourists. Data on nights spent in tourist accommodation establishments by month are also presented for NUTS level 2 regions.

In 2024, there were 3.02 [billion](/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Billion "Glossary:Billion") nights spent in tourist accommodation across the EU, 51.9% of which were accounted for by domestic tourists and a slightly smaller share by international tourists (48.1%). The total number of nights spent in EU tourist accommodation increased by 2.7% between 2023 and 2024, with a faster growth rate for nights spent by international tourists (5.5%) than for domestic tourists (0.2%).

**Map 1** presents information for NUTS level 3 regions on the total number of nights spent in tourist accommodation during 2024 (as denoted by the size of each circle). There were 11 regions in the EU where the total number of nights spent exceeded 30.0 million:

- the Spanish island regions of Mallorca (55.3 million nights spent) and Tenerife (35.8 million)
- the capital regions of Roma in Italy (47.2 million), Paris in France (43.2 million), Madrid in Spain (32.3 million) and Berlin in Germany (30.4 million)
- the Spanish coastal regions of Barcelona (41.2 million), Alicante/Alacant (32.6 million) and Málaga (30.5 million)
- the coastal region of Venezia (38.8 million) and the mountainous region of Bolzano-Bozen (37.0 million), both in Italy.

**Map 1** also provides information on the origin of EU tourists, identifying (according to the colour of each circle), regions where:

- **international tourists** accounted for a majority of the total nights spent
- **domestic tourists** accounted for a majority of the total nights spent.

While domestic tourists accounted for approximately half of all nights spent in EU tourist accommodation in 2024, they frequented a much wider range of destinations than international tourists. Indeed, nights spent by domestic tourists outnumbered those spent by international tourists in the vast majority of EU regions (936 out of the 1 102 regions for which data are available).


- coastal regions (principally located in the Mediterranean)
- mountainous regions (predominantly in the Alps)
- capital regions (across a broad range of EU countries).

Many of these 93 regions with a high concentration of international tourists experience pronounced seasonal peaks in demand, typically during the summer and/or winter months, which may create tourism pressures and have implications for sustainable development, as well as for the preservation and protection of natural and urban environments (see below for more information on seasonality).

[iframe](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/statistics_explained/maps/regional-yearbook-2026/tourism/nights-spent-tourist-accommodation-2024.html)

Map 1: Nights spent in tourist accommodation  
*Source:* Eurostat ([tour_occ_nin3](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/783347bd-f2b9-4984-8f11-014f806e273a?lang=en))

***Mallorca recorded the highest number of nights spent by international tourists in 2024, while Berlin recorded the highest number for domestic tourists***

**Figure 1** shows the most frequented tourist destinations in the EU, based on NUTS level 3 regions. It provides information for those regions with the highest numbers of nights spent in tourist accommodation, detailing the most frequented regions for all tourists, for domestic tourists and for international tourists.

Capital regions serve as economic, political and financial hubs, attracting professionals for meetings, conferences and other corporate activities. They are also cultural destinations, offering historical sites, museums, concert venues, theatres and stadia. As such, capital regions function as both business and cultural centres. In 2024, the EU regions with the highest numbers of nights spent by domestic tourists included:

- Berlin in Germany (17.6 million)
- Paris in France (15.3 million)
- Madrid in Spain (14.5 million)
- Roma in Italy (13.3 million).

Following these 4 capital regions in the EU’s largest economies, the highest levels of nights spent by domestic tourists were primarily recorded in coastal and mountainous regions of the larger EU countries. In 2024, domestic tourists spent at least 11.0 million nights in:

- Hérault (12.3 million) and Var (12.0 million) along France’s southern coast, which include popular destinations such as Montpellier, Sète, Saint-Tropez and Fréjus
- Hamburg (12.3 million) in northern Germany, a major port known for its maritime heritage, cultural attractions and vibrant neighbourhoods
- Alicante/Alacant (12.1 million) on the south-eastern coast of Spain, including popular destinations such as Benidorm, Altea or Calpe
- Trento (11.0 million) in northern Italy, a popular destination for mountain tourism, including skiing and hiking.

In 2024, the Spanish island region of Mallorca had, by far, the highest number of nights spent in tourist accommodation by international tourists, at 51.2 million. There were 4 other EU regions where international tourists spent at least 30.0 million nights:

- the Italian regions of Roma (33.9 million) and Venezia (30.0 million)
- the Spanish regions of Barcelona (31.4 million) and Tenerife (31.3 million).

The regions with the next highest numbers of nights spent by international tourists were more geographically diverse, with at least 20.0 million nights spent in:

- the Spanish island/coastal regions of Gran Canaria, Málaga and Alicante/Alacant
- the coastal regions of Istarska županija (Croatia) and Kalymnos and its surrounding islands (Greece)
- the capital regions of Paris (France) and Groot-Amsterdam (the Netherlands)
- the mountainous region of Bolzano-Bozen in northern Italy.

**Figure 2** presents, for each EU country, the most frequented region by domestic and by international tourists (based on the regional share of the total number of nights spent in each country). These relative shares reflect, to some degree, the number of regions in each EU country; Cyprus and Luxembourg are single regions at NUTS level 3 (and hence are not shown).

In 2024, there were 11 EU countries (out of 25 for which data are presented) where the same region was the most frequented by both domestic and international tourists. In Denmark, Germany, Estonia, France, Italy, Latvia, Malta, Finland and Sweden this was the capital region: Byen København, Berlin, Põhja-Eesti, Paris, Roma, Rīga, the island of Malta, Helsinki-Uusimaa and Stockholms län. In Bulgaria and Portugal, the most frequented region by both domestic and international tourists was a coastal region: Burgas on the Black Sea coast and the Algarve on the Atlantic coast.

In more than half of the remaining EU countries (9 out of 14), the capital region was the most frequented region by international tourists in 2024. This was the case in Belgium, Czechia, Ireland, Lithuania, Hungary, the Netherlands, Austria, Romania and Slovakia. In the other 5 countries, the most frequented regions for international tourists included:

- the coastal regions of Kalymnos, Karpathos, Kasos, Kos, Rodos (Greece), Mallorca (Spain) and Istarska županija (Croatia)
- the historic and cultural region of Miasto Kraków (Poland)
- the mountainous region of Gorenjska (Slovenia), which includes the popular tourist attraction of Lake Bled.

Among the 14 EU countries where different regions were most frequented by domestic and by international tourists, domestic tourism in 2024 was often concentrated in regions that are less well-known internationally. Leaving aside the 4 landlocked countries, only 2 of the most frequented regions were not coastal: the capital region of Madrid in Spain and the forested region of Veluwe in the Netherlands. Elsewhere, the following coastal regions recorded the highest numbers of nights spent by domestic tourists:

- Prov. West-Vlaanderen in Belgium (North Sea)
- South-West in Ireland (Atlantic Ocean)
- Andros, Thira, Kea, Milos, Mykonos, Naxos, Paros, Syros, Tinos in Greece (Aegean Sea, eastern Mediterranean)
- Primorsko-goranska županija in Croatia and Obalno-kraška in Slovenia (Adriatic Sea)
- Klaipėdos apskritis in Lithuania and Koszaliński in Poland (Baltic Sea)
- Constanţa in Romania (Black Sea).

In the 4 landlocked countries, the highest numbers of nights spent by domestic tourists in 2024 were recorded in:

- Královéhradecký kraj in Czechia, Pinzgau-Pongau in Austria and Prešovský kraj in Slovakia, all relatively mountainous regions
- Veszprém in Hungary, a cultural and historic region that includes wine-growing areas around Lake Balaton.

## Seasonality

Seasonality has a considerable impact on tourism. It is linked to various environmental factors, such as climate or geographical location, as well as socio-economic factors like public and school holidays or factories closing for annual leave. Tourist arrivals are generally more evenly spread than the number of nights spent across the calendar year, due to a higher concentration of longer stays in the summer months.

**More about the data: reading a coxcomb map**

A coxcomb map (sometimes referred to as a rose chart or a polar area chart) displays values as slices extending outwards from a central point. Each slice represents a category, often a time period such as a month (as in **Map 2**), and is used to show how values change over time. For a monthly presentation, the full circle is divided into 12 equal segments, 1 for each month. The months are read clockwise starting from 12 o’clock, beginning with January and ending with December.

For these monthly tourism data, there are 2 stacked components representing nights spent by domestic tourists and by international tourists. Comparing total areas across the months reveals seasonal patterns (for example, higher numbers in July and August), while comparing the radial components within each month shows the relative contributions of domestic and international tourists.

***More than half of all nights spent in EU tourist accommodation in 2024 occurred between June and September***

As noted above, a total of 3.02 billion nights were spent in EU tourist accommodation in 2024. The highest shares were recorded in the summer months, peaking at 16.4% in August and 15.0% in July, while June (10.5%) and September (10.0%) were the only other months to record double-digit shares. By contrast, the lowest shares were recorded in January (4.5%) and November (4.8%).

**Map 2** highlights the most frequented tourist regions in the EU, detailing both the seasonal component and the breakdown by origin of tourist. It confirms the relatively high share of nights spent by international tourists in southern/Mediterranean regions, with domestic tourists accounting for a majority of nights spent across most western, northern and eastern EU countries, with the notable exception of several capital regions that attract large numbers of international tourists.

Looking in more detail at each month in 2024, the following NUTS level 2 regions recorded the highest numbers of nights spent in tourist accommodation by domestic and international tourists combined:

- January – Canarias (Spain), Ile-de-France and Rhône-Alpes (both France)
- February – Canarias, Rhône-Alpes and Tirol (Austria)
- March – Canarias, Ile-de-France and Andalucía (Spain)
- April – Canarias, Ile-de-France and Andalucía
- May – Illes Balears, Cataluña (both Spain) and Ile-de-France
- June – Jadranska Hrvatska (Croatia), Illes Balears and Cataluña
- July – Jadranska Hrvatska, Cataluña and Veneto (Italy)
- August – Jadranska Hrvatska, Cataluña and Veneto
- September – Illes Balears, Jadranska Hrvatska and Cataluña
- October – Canarias, Illes Balears and Ile-de-France
- November – Canarias, Ile-de-France and Andalucía
- December – Canarias, Ile-de-France and Rhône-Alpes

***Languedoc-Roussillon in southern France recorded the highest number of nights spent by domestic tourists during the summer of 2024***

A closer examination of the data shown in **Map 2** reveals that the south-eastern French region of Rhône-Alpes had the highest number of nights spent by domestic tourists in January, February and March 2024, reflecting the popularity of the Alps during the winter tourism season. The French capital region of Ile-de-France was the most frequented NUTS level 2 region by domestic tourists in April, October, November and December 2024, likely reflecting short city breaks, as well as professional visits.

The northern German region of Schleswig-Holstein, with its Baltic and North Sea coastlines, recorded the highest number of nights spent by domestic tourists in May 2024, while the central Italian region of Emilia-Romagna, which includes several Adriatic beach resorts (for example, Rimini), recorded the highest count in June 2024. During the peak summer period of July and August 2024, the southern French coastal region of Languedoc-Roussillon recorded the highest number of nights spent by domestic tourists, while the southern Spanish region of Andalucía had the highest count in September 2024.

***Jadranska Hrvatska on the Croatian Adriatic coastline recorded the highest number of nights spent by international tourists in the height of summer 2024***

Turning to the most frequented NUTS level 2 regions among international tourists, Canarias in Spain recorded the highest number of nights spent in January to April 2024 and again in October to December 2024, reflecting its year-round appeal and relatively stable temperatures. During these months, the number of nights spent by international tourists ranged between 6.8 million and 8.1 million.


The Spanish island region of Illes Balears recorded the highest number of nights spent by international tourists in May 2024, with visitors to islands such as Mallorca and Ibiza benefitting from the favourable spring climate before the peak summer influx of tourists.

[iframe](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/GISCO/maps/regional-yearbook/2026/CH10/CH10M02.html)

Map 2: Nights spent in tourist accommodation  
*Source:* Eurostat ([tour_occ_nin2m](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9d52e0bf-a7c9-40fc-b91f-a85e352431a0?lang=en)) and ([tour_occ_nim](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a4adda51-a806-4692-9d7f-0f730aafb819?lang=en))

**Map 3** highlights the peak month for tourism in 2024 among tourists (domestic and international combined) across NUTS level 2 regions.

- In the vast majority of regions – as was the case for the EU as a whole – August was the busiest month of the year; this was the case in 176 out of the 244 regions for which data are available.
- July was the busiest month for 48 of the remaining regions across the EU, while no other month recorded a double-digit count
- October had the next highest figure, with 6 regions – half of which were capitals – reporting their highest number of nights spent during this month
- March, April and November did not feature and were not the busiest tourism month in any of the NUTS level 2 regions.

February 2024 was the busiest tourism month of the year in 3 western regions of Austria, namely, Tirol (5.7 million nights spent in tourist accommodation), Salzburg (3.7 million nights) and Vorarlberg (1.1 million nights). The only other regions to report February 2024 as their busiest tourism month of the year were the Bulgarian capital region of Yugozapaden (0.5 million nights) and the French outermost region of Guadeloupe (148 000 nights, reflecting the dry season and its warm tropical climate). Similar seasonal patterns were observed in other outermost regions, with peak demand in January for Martinique, May for Mayotte, and October for both La Réunion and Guyane.

August 2024 was the busiest tourism month across most southern, western and eastern regions of the EU, although capital regions often proved to be an exception, for example:

- in the Bulgarian capital region of Yugozapaden, February recorded the highest number of nights spent in tourist accommodation
- in the Irish capital region of Eastern and Midland, June was the busiest tourism month
- in the Belgian, German, Italian and Slovak capital regions of Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest, Berlin, Lazio and Bratislavský kraj, July was the busiest
- in the Spanish, French and Romanian capital regions of Comunidad de Madrid, Ile-de-France and Bucureşti-Ilfov, October recorded the highest number of nights spent in tourist accommodation
- in the Austrian capital region of Wien, December was the busiest month.

In northern regions of the EU, July was generally the busiest tourism month of the year. This pattern was also observed in the capital regions of Hovedstaden, Helsinki-Uusimaa and Stockholm, as well as in Estonia and Latvia. The only exceptions were in Lithuania, where both regions reported their busiest tourism month as August.

Seasonal tourism demand was highly concentrated in many regions across the EU. In 2024, 35.5% of all nights spent in the Romanian coastal region of Sud-Est on the Black Sea were recorded in August. Very high shares were also observed in the southern Italian region of Calabria (32.2% in August) and in the south-eastern Bulgarian coastal region of Yugoiztochen (30.5%). In the Nordic EU countries, 32.0% of the total nights spent in the southern Swedish region of Småland med öarna (which includes the island of Öland) were recorded in July, while a similarly high share was observed in the Finnish archipelago of Åland (30.6).

Map 3: Busiest tourist month  
*Source:* Eurostat ([tour_occ_nin2m](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9d52e0bf-a7c9-40fc-b91f-a85e352431a0?lang=en)) and ([tour_occ_nim](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a4adda51-a806-4692-9d7f-0f730aafb819?lang=en))

## Tourism pressures

Since the expansion of mass tourism in the 1950s and 1960s, EU regions have experienced tourism growth in markedly different ways. Some regions continue to attract relatively few visitors, while others have seen substantial increases in visitor numbers. These developments have been shaped by structural changes within the tourism sector, including the emergence of package holidays, the growth of low-cost air travel, the rise of online booking platforms and the diversification of accommodation (for example, the emergence of short-term rental platforms). More recently, tourism patterns have also been influenced by changing work and mobility patterns, including the gradual rise of remote working and digital nomadism, which has contributed to longer stays in certain destinations.

In the EU, tourism policy has increasingly focused on sustainability and resilience, in line with initiatives such as the [European Green Deal](https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal_en) and the [Transition pathway for tourism](https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/404a8144-8892-11ec-8c40-01aa75ed71a1). These frameworks emphasise the need to:

- balance economic activity with the protection of cultural and natural heritage
- improve environmental performance
- support the digital and green transformation of the sector.

Sustainable tourism encompasses the preservation and enhancement of cultural assets, including the arts and gastronomy, as well as the protection of natural environments and biodiversity. The quality and long-term attractiveness of tourism destinations are closely linked to their environmental integrity and their integration within local communities. For the purpose of this publication, tourism intensity is defined as the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation per 1 000 inhabitants.

***For every 1 000 inhabitants in the EU, an average of 6 725 nights were spent in tourist accommodation during 2024***

In 2024, there were 6 725 nights spent in EU tourist accommodation per 1 000 inhabitants. The regional distribution of tourism intensity was heavily skewed, indicating that mass tourism tends to be concentrated in relatively few regions. The ratio of tourist nights per 1 000 inhabitants was higher than the EU average in fewer than 3 out of 10 NUTS level 3 regions (318 out of 1 117 for which data are available). The statistics presented are likely to underestimate the full extent of tourism pressures, as the numerator does not include same-day visitors, some short-term stays booked via online platforms or stays in non-rented accommodation such as second homes or with friends/relatives.

**Map 4** shows EU regions experiencing the highest tourism intensity in 2024. A total of 123 NUTS level 3 regions recorded at least 15 000 nights spent in tourist accommodation per 1 000 inhabitants (as indicated by the darkest shade). Many of the regions in this group were located along coastlines or within a corridor extending from southern France through the Alps to western Austria, while others were characterised by their very low population density (for example, the northernmost region of Finland, Lappi).

At the upper end of the distribution, 9 regions exceeded 100 000 nights per 1 000 inhabitants:

- Zakynthos, a Greek island region in the Ionian Sea, recorded the highest tourism intensity (162 700 nights per 1 000 inhabitants)
- Istarska županija on the Adriatic coast in Croatia recorded the second highest ratio (132 400 nights per 1 000 inhabitants)
- 3 additional Greek island regions also featured among those regions with the highest values
  * Kalymnos, Karpathos – Iroiki Nisos Kasos, Kos and Rodos in the Aegean Sea (130 000 nights per 1 000 inhabitants)
  * Kerkyra in the Ionian Sea (102 700 nights per 1 000 inhabitants)
  * Andros, Thira, Kea, Milos, Mykonos, Naxos, Paros, Syros and Tinos (also in the Aegean Sea; 100 600 nights per 1 000 inhabitants)
- Fuerteventura and Lanzarote in the Spanish region of Canarias recorded the next highest ratios (128 100 and 120 100 nights per 1 000 inhabitants, respectively)
- 2 mountainous regions in western Austria also recorded very high tourism intensity, Tiroler Oberland and Pinzgau-Pongau (116 300 nights and 109 800 nights per 1 000 inhabitants, respectively).


- Poland (29 regions) – with the north-eastern region of Ostrołęcki recording its lowest ratio, at 340 nights spent in tourist accommodation per 1 000 inhabitants
- Romania (24 regions), with the southern region of Teleorman having the lowest ratio in the EU, at 19 nights per 1 000 inhabitants
- Germany (19 regions), with the western city of Herne in North Rhine-Westphalia recording its lowest ratio, at 393 nights per 1 000 inhabitants
- Bulgaria (13 regions), with the western region of Pernik having its lowest ratio, at 320 nights per 1 000 inhabitants
- Belgium (11 regions), with Arr. Soignies, located to the north-east of Mons in the Hainaut region, recording its lowest ratio, at 349 nights per 1 000 inhabitants.

Together with Teleorman in Romania, the Greek region of Dytikos Tomeas Athinon – a densely populated region to the west of the capital, largely composed of industrial and/or residential neighbourhoods – was the only other region in the EU with fewer than 100 tourist nights per 1 000 inhabitants in 2024.

[iframe](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/statistics_explained/maps/regional-yearbook-2026/tourism/nights-spent-tourist-accommodation-relative-resident-population-2024.html)

Map 4: Nights spent in tourist accommodation  
*Source:* Eurostat ([tour_occ_nin3](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7a2683de-16b4-415c-87d3-da50e83a4341?lang=en)) and ([tour_occ_ninat](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/34e92002-46ac-407d-8c6e-289fdce3a175?lang=en))

***In 2024, tourism density in the EU stood at 715 nights per square kilometre***

An alternative indicator for analysing tourism pressures is tourism density, defined here as the total number of nights spent in tourist accommodation per square kilometre (km²) of area. In 2024, the EU average was 715 nights spent per km².

**Map 5** shows that tourism density was often concentrated in predominantly urban regions, which generally have much smaller areas. In 2024, 115 NUTS level 3 regions had a ratio of at least 5 000 nights spent per km² (as shown by the darkest shade). The French capital region of Paris was a clear outlier, recording by far the highest concentration of tourists in 2024, with 419 000 nights spent per km². This was 4.6 times as high as in any other region of the EU: the Greek capital region – Kentrikos Tomeas Athinon – had the second highest ratio, with 90 900 nights spent per km².

There were 20 NUTS level 3 regions in the EU where the ratio of tourism density was higher than 20 000 nights spent per km² in 2024. Half of this group consisted of capital regions: those of France and Greece (already mentioned above), together with the capital regions of Denmark, Austria, Belgium, Malta, Czechia, the Netherlands, Germany and Hungary. Particularly high ratios were also recorded in:

- 6 predominantly urban regions of Germany – München, Frankfurt am Main, Düsseldorf, Hamburg, Stuttgart and Nürnberg
- the suburban region of Hauts-de-Seine located to the west of the French capital
- the island region of Lanzarote that forms part of Canarias in Spain
- Miasto Kraków in Poland, a major cultural and short-break destination
- Venezia in Italy, a historic city.

At the other end of the distribution, 115 regions had tourism density ratios below 75 nights per km² in 2024 (as shown by the lightest shade in **Map 5**). These regions were generally concentrated in rural territories of northern, eastern and southern EU countries. The only regions in western EU countries were the French regions of Haute-Saône, Meuse (both in eastern France), Creuse (central France) and Guyane (an outermost region).

At the very bottom of the distribution, 3 regions recorded particularly low tourism density ratios in 2024: Călăraşi and Teleorman in southern Romania, as well as Guyane, each with fewer than 10 nights per km².

Following the convention for international tourism statistics, we exclude international airfare from the calculation of wellness tourism. The international airfare paid by international tourists does not necessarily accrue to the country they are visiting. Therefore, expenditures on international airfare are typically not included in the tourism receipts reported by individual countries, but instead are covered in a different line item in national balance of payment statistics.
Our wellness tourism estimates include trips and expenditures made by both international and domestic travelers:
• International wellness tourism expenditures: All receipts earned by a country from inbound wellness tourists visiting from abroad, with an overnight stay.

Global Wellness Summit | Global Wellness Institute | Press Image Gallery | Press Release Archive

**New Research From the Global Wellness Institute Ranks Italy Among the World’s Top 10 Wellness Economies, Valued at $140.6 Billion

**
The new research, made possible through a partnership with Italcares Federterme, highlights a nearly $27 billion market for wellness tourism, spa, and thermal springs
Miami, FL – February 3, 2026 – For the first time, the Global Wellness Institute (GWI), the leading non-profit research organization for the global wellness industry, has released comprehensive data on Italy’s wellness economy, revealing a market valued at $140.6 billion and ranking 10th globally and 4th in Europe.
The 2025 Global Wellness Economy: Italy report is now available on GWI’s Geography of Wellness platform, made possible through a new partnership with Italcares , a digital platform created by Federterme that connects international patients and wellness travelers with Italy’s leading healthcare and thermal facilities.
The new research analyzes Italy’s performance across all 11 sectors in the global wellness economy. Italy ranks among the top ten global markets in ten of these categories, including physical activity; healthy eating, nutrition and weight loss; mental wellness; workplace wellness; traditional and complementary medicine; public health, prevention and personalized medicine; personal care and beauty; wellness tourism; spas; and thermal and mineral springs. Together, Italy’s wellness tourism, spa, and thermal/mineral springs sectors approached $27 billion in 2024.
“Italy represents one of the most mature and integrated wellness markets in the world,” said Susie Ellis, chair and CEO of the Global Wellness Institute. “Its deep heritage in thermalism and preventive medicine, combined with strong public–private collaboration and world-class natural and medical assets, positions Italy not just as a wellness destination, but as a global model for health and longevity.”
The report highlights Italy’s five largest wellness sectors: personal care and beauty ($38.43 billion); healthy eating, nutrition and weight loss ($25.93 billion); physical activity ($21.25 billion); wellness tourism ($19.99 billion); and public health, prevention and personalized medicine ($12.4 billion).

# The European market potential for wellness tourism

Last updated:

30 September 2026

Takes 25 minutes to read

The European wellness tourism market offers strong opportunities for tourism businesses in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Demand for wellness travel is growing. More and more European travellers are seeking holidays that improve their physical and mental wellbeing. Nature-based experiences, healthy lifestyles, sustainability and authentic local culture are shaping the future of the wellness tourism market.

## 1. Product description: wellness tourism

Wellness tourism is travel that helps people improve or maintain their physical, mental, emotional, spiritual or social wellbeing. Wellness tourism has traditionally been associated with spas and relaxation. However, today’s wellness travellers look for a much wider range of experiences.

Many travellers use wellness holidays to reduce stress, improve fitness, reconnect with nature, sleep better, adopt healthier lifestyles and escape busy daily routines. Wellness tourism includes everything from yoga retreats to nature-based experiences.

Figure 1: Dimensions of wellness

![Diagram showing the dimensions of wellnes](/sites/default/files/2026-09/Figure%201%20-%20Dimensions%20of%20wellness.png)

Source: [GWI, Global Wellness Economy Monitor, 2025](https://globalwellnessinstitute.org/industry-research/2025-global-wellness-economy-monitor/)

The table below provides examples of common wellness tourism products and the dimensions of wellbeing they support.

Ayurvedic spa therapies at [Sen Wellness Sanctuary](https://www.senwellnesssanctuary.com/), Sri Lanka. [Namia River Retreat](https://namiariverretreat.com/) in Vietnam features daily wellness journeys with hydrotherapy and traditional Vietnamese therapies. [Banyan Tree Lang Co](https://www.banyantree.com/vietnam/lang-co), Vietnam, offers detox retreats, fitness activities and holistic Asian healing rituals. | Physical and mental wellbeing                           |

[Manda de Laos](https://www.mandadelaos.com/), Laos, offers traditional Lao massage and herbal therapies inspired by local healing traditions. | Physical, emotional, spiritual and social wellbeing     |

Source: Acorn Tourism Consulting, 2026

Many tourism businesses already offer products that contribute to visitor wellbeing. They do this even if they do not market themselves as wellness tourism providers. Nature-based tourism, adventure tourism, community-based tourism, cultural experiences and healthy local cuisine can all form part of a wellness tourism offer. This creates opportunities for suppliers in LMICs to attract wellness travellers without having to develop dedicated wellness resorts or retreat programmes.

### End market segmentation

Wellness travellers are not a single market segment. They have different motivations and spending patterns. Wellbeing does not play the same role in all wellness travellers’ decisions. Understanding these differences can help tourism businesses develop suitable products and identify the most relevant market opportunities.

#### Primary and secondary wellness trips

Wellness tourism includes both primary and secondary wellness trips. In primary wellness trips, wellness is the main purpose of travel. In secondary wellness trips, wellness activities are part of a wider holiday or business trip. You can see in the chart below that secondary wellness tourism accounts for almost 85% of the market, in terms of both trips and expenditure.

Figure 2: Breakdown of Wellness Trips: Primary Versus Secondary (2024)

![Graph showing the breakdown of wellness trips - primary versus secondary (2024)](/sites/default/files/2026-09/Figure%202%20-%20Breakdown%20of%20wellness%20trips%20-%20primary%20versus%20secondary%20%282024%29.png)

Source: [GWI, Global Wellness Economy Monitor, 2025](https://globalwellnessinstitute.org/industry-research/2025-global-wellness-economy-monitor/)

As such, it is clear that the greatest potential lies in secondary wellness tourism. It shows that most wellness tourism is not made up of dedicated spa or retreat holidays. Instead, travellersmake wellness activities part of broader leisure trips more and more often. Primary and secondary wellness travellers are also motivated differently, as explained below.

Table 2: Primary and secondary wellness travellers

| Type                   | Primary wellness traveller                                                                                                                                                                              | Secondary wellness traveller                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Description            | Wellness is the main purpose of travel. They choose a destination, accommodation or programme for its wellbeing benefits.                                                                               | Wellness activities enhance a wider holiday experience for secondary wellness travellers, but they are not the main reason for travel.                                                                   |
| Typical traveller goal | Improve health, reduce stress, improve sleep, increase fitness, support healthy ageing.                                                                                                                 | Relax, recharge, connect with nature and enjoy healthy experiences while on holiday.                                                                                                                     |
| Examples               | Wellness retreats Yoga and meditation retreats Fitness retreats Detox and nutrition programmes Holistic healing retreats Longevity and preventative health programmes Wellness resorts and spa retreats | Spa treatments during a beach holiday Yoga sessions at a safari lodge Mindfulness activities as part of a nature holiday Healthy local cuisine during a cultural tour Forest bathing during an ecotourism experience Traditional healing experiences alongside other tourism activities |

Source: Global Wellness Institute/ Acorn Tourism Consulting, 2026

### Domestic and international wellness travel

Wellness tourism is segmented into domestic and international travel. Globally, [domestic wellness tourism is much larger. It accounted for 87% of wellness trips in 2024](https://globalwellnessinstitute.org/industry-research/2025-global-wellness-economy-monitor/). International wellness trips accounted for 13%. It is interesting that LATAM, Africa and MEA rely on more international wellness arrivals than Europe and North America.

Figure 3: Breakdown of wellness trips: international versus domestic, 2024

![Graph showing the breakdown of wellness trips - international versus domestic, 2024](/sites/default/files/2026-09/Figure%203%20-%20Breakdown%20of%20wellness%20trips%20-%20international%20versus%20domestic%2C%202024.png)

Source: [GWI, Global Wellness Economy Monitor, 2025](https://globalwellnessinstitute.org/industry-research/2025-global-wellness-economy-monitor/)

The industry should not ignore domestic tourism. It can provide a more stable market and support year-round demand. It can also help businesses test and refine wellness products before targeting international visitors. Despite this, international wellness travellers are still important because they tend to spend more per trip. GWI estimates that international wellness tourists spend 38% more per trip than the average international tourist. Domestic wellness tourists spend 137% more per trip than the average domestic tourist.

Figure 4: Wellness tourism spending premiums, 2024

![Graph showing wellness tourism spending premiums, 2024](/sites/default/files/2026-09/Figure%204%20-%20Wellness%20tourism%20spending%20premiums%2C%202024.png)

Source: [GWI, Global Wellness Economy Monitor, 2025](https://globalwellnessinstitute.org/industry-research/2025-global-wellness-economy-monitor/)

#### Affluent wellness travellers

Wellness tourism can also be segmented by traveller profile and spending power. Affluent (wealthy) travellers are an important target market. They are more likely to purchase premium wellness products and are willing to spend more on health and wellbeing experiences.

Research among [affluent international travellers found that 54% had taken a dedicated wellness holiday](https://altiant.com/luxury-insights-2025), while 69% had booked wellness activities as part of a broader trip. This highlights the broad appeal of wellness experiences across different types of holidays. It also demonstrates opportunities to incorporate wellness elements into mainstream tourism products.

Figure 5: Willingness to spend on wellness holidays

![Graph showing the willingness to spend on wellness holidays](/sites/default/files/2026-09/Figure%205%20-%20Willingness%20to%20spend%20on%20wellness%20holidays.png)

Source: Altiant/LuxuryOpinions, 2025

Affluent travellers are also willing to spend more on wellness experiences. 92% of affluent travellers would be willing to pay a premium for a wellness holiday. This shows the large commercial potential of wellness tourism and its ability to increase visitor spending.

### Accessible tourism in the European market

Accessible tourism is the ongoing endeavour to ensure tourist destinations, products and services are accessible to all people, regardless of their physical limitations, disabilities or age. It encompasses publicly and privately owned tourist locations. The improvements not only benefit those with permanent physical disabilities, but also parents with small children, elderly travellers, people with temporary injuries such as a broken leg, and their travel companions. Disabled tourists may travel individually, in groups, with their family or with carers.

#### Accessibility and wellness tourism

Wellness tourism should be accessible to everyone. Travellers with disabilities, mobility limitations, sensory impairments, chronic health conditions and older travellers seek out wellness experiences more and more often. This means that accessible wellness tourism can help businesses reach a wider market while providing more inclusive experiences.

To attract wellness travellers with accessibility needs, it is important to communicate clearly about your facilities, services and activities. Travellers will research extensively before booking. They need accurate information to determine whether a wellness experience would suit their needs. Some best practices include:

- Clearly describe the accessibility of accommodation, wellness facilities and treatment areas. This includes access routes, bathrooms, pools and spa facilities.
- Ensure staff understand different accessibility requirements and can respond to enquiries appropriately before and during a trip.
- Offer flexibility where possible. For example, adapt activities, treatment schedules and wellness programmes to individual needs where you can.
- Provide detailed information about the physical requirements of wellness activities, such as yoga sessions, hiking trails, meditation programmes and fitness classes.
- Consider offering alternative wellness experiences for guests with limited mobility or other accessibility requirements.
- Ensure information is available in accessible formats and that communication is clear and easy to understand.

Tip:

- Read the CBI study, [What are the opportunities in the European market for accessible tourism?](https://www.cbi.eu/market-information/tourism/accessible-tourism), for practical and useful advice to make your tours accessible.

Tips:

- Review your existing offering and see how it fits. You may already be a wellness tourism provider without knowing it. Nature-based tourism, adventure activities, healthy local cuisine, traditional healing practices and cultural experiences can all form part of a wellness offer.
- Focus on secondary wellness tourism. Most European wellness travellers are not looking for a dedicated spa or retreat holiday. They want wellness experiences as part of a wider trip. You do not need to specialise in wellness alone to attract this market.

## 2. What makes Europe an interesting market for wellness tourism?

Europe is an interesting market for wellness tourism. It is one of the world’s most important wellness markets. It has a long tradition of spa, health, active and nature-based travel. European consumers are also familiar with many wellness products and experiences. They are treating travel as an investment in their health more and more often. They do not just aim to rest but to come home feeling physically better, mentally restored and better equipped for daily life. Travel that supports this has become a mainstream expectation rather than a niche preference.

The global wellness tourism market is very large. It was valued at $893.9 billion (USD) in 2024. It is forecast to reach $1.4 trillion by 2029, growing at an average annual rate of 9.1%. The chart below shows that wellness tourism is a substantial part of the global wellness market.

Figure 6: Global Wellness Economy, 2024

![Diagram showing the Global wellness economy in 2024](/sites/default/files/2026-09/Figure%206%20-%20Global%20wellness%20economy%2C%202024.jpg)

Source: GWI, Global Wellness Economy Monitor, 2025

Europe was the second-largest wellness tourism market, in terms of both expenditure ($258.2 billion (USD)) and the number of trips (348.4 million) in 2024. This strong wellness culture is also reflected in travel behaviour. Europe accounted for more wellness tourism trips than North America. It also generated more wellness tourism expenditure after the Asia-Pacific region.

Although these figures include both domestic and international travel, they provide a useful indication of market maturity and consumer engagement with wellness tourism.

Table 3: Wellness Tourism Trips and Expenditure by Region, 2024

| Region                   | Wellness tourism expenditure, 2024 (US$) | Average annual growth rate (2019-2024) | Number of wellness tourism trips, 2024 | Average expenditure per trip, 2024 (US$) |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| North America            | $346.9 billion                           | 5.8%                                   | 239.3 million                          | $1,449                                   |
| Europe                   | $258.2 billion                           | 5.0%                                   | 348.4 million                          | $741                                     |
| Asia-Pacific             | $215.0 billion                           | 8.9%                                   | 562.7 million                          | $382                                     |
| Latin America-Caribbean  | $41.0 billion                            | 4.8%                                   | 60.0 million                           | $683                                     |
| Middle East-North Africa | $24.7 billion                            | 15.0%                                  | 19.7 million                           | $1,257                                   |
| Sub-Saharan Africa       | $6.9 billion                             | 6.6%                                   | 9.0 million                            | $908                                     |
| World: Wellness Tourism  | $893.9 billion                           | 6.4%                                   | 1,239.0 million                        | $721                                     |
| World: ALL Tourism       | $5,066.5 billion                         | 1.9%                                   | 14,895.2 million                       | $340                                     |

Source: GWI, Global Wellness Economy Monitor, 2025

The European interest in wellness tourism can also be seen in CBI’s research across six European source markets. 50% of travellers cited relaxation and escape from routine as one of their main motivations for travel. The figure was particularly high among Dutch (69%), German (52%) and British travellers (47%).

The same research found that 32% of European travellers consider free time for relaxation an important factor when choosing a holiday destination. The figure was 52% among Dutch travellers, 38% among British travellers and 36% among German travellers.

These findings suggest that many European travellers do not seek out dedicated wellness holidays. Instead, they look for travel experiences that help them relax, reduce stress, reconnect with nature and return home feeling healthier and more balanced.

Many LMICs already have the natural and cultural assets that European wellness travellers want. Biodiversity, traditional wellbeing practices, healthy local cuisine, year-round climates, outdoor lifestyles and strong cultural traditions provide a natural foundation for wellness tourism, often without the need for major investment in purpose-built facilities.

Tips:

- Build on existing assets, such as nature, outdoor activities, healthy local cuisine and traditional wellbeing practices. Do not immediately invest in purpose-built wellness facilities.
- Communicate the wellbeing benefits of your experiences clearly. European wellness travellers seek outcomes, such as relaxation, stress reduction, improved fitness and a stronger connection with nature.
- Consider adding simple wellness elements to existing tourism products, such as guided mindfulness activities, healthy food options or wellness treatments.
- Position wellness experiences as part of a wider holiday offer. Many European travellers make wellness activities part of nature, cultural, adventure and beach holidays.

## 3. Which European countries offer the most opportunities for wellness tourism?

Europe is one of the world’s largest source regions for wellness tourism. However, opportunities vary between markets. Some countries have larger, more mature wellness tourism sectors. This means they have stronger consumer engagement in wellness travel and are more familiar with wellness products and experiences.

Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy, Spain and Austria are Europe’s most established wellness tourism markets. The figures in the table below include both domestic and international wellness tourism. As a result, they do not measure outbound demand directly. However, they provide a useful indication of market maturity, consumer participation in wellness travel and the overall importance of wellness tourism within each market.

Table 4: Selected European source markets for wellness tourism, 2024

| Country        | Wellness tourism trips (million) | Wellness tourism expenditure (USD) |
| -------------- | -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Germany        | 77.2 million                     | 40.6 billion                       |
| France         | 41.5 million                     | 45.6 billion                       |
| United Kingdom | 22.3 million                     | 19.1 billion                       |
| Italy          | 11.5 million                     | 20.0 billion                       |
| Spain          | 20.8 million                     | 16.7 billion                       |
| Austria        | 18.4 million                     | 18.3 billion                       |
| Switzerland    | 12.0 million                     | 18.8 billion                       |

Source: [GWI, Global Wellness Economy Monitor, 2025](https://globalwellnessinstitute.org/industry-research/2025-global-wellness-economy-monitor/)

### Germany

Germany is Europe’s largest wellness tourism market. It recorded 77.2 million wellness tourism trips and $40.6 billion (USD) in wellness tourism expenditure in 2024. Wellness has been part of German culture for a long time. This is thanks to thermal baths, health resorts, saunas and the traditional Kur system: a preventative health retreat.

With more than 350 recognised health spas and resorts, German travellers are familiar with wellness products and expect high standards of quality, professionalism and measurable wellbeing benefits.

Figure 7: A winter sauna experience in Germany

![Interior shot of a sauna in a snowy area](/sites/default/files/styles/image_medium/public/2026-09/STOCK_Figure%207%20-%20A%20winter%20sauna%20experience%20in%20Germany.jpg)

Source: [HUUM, Unsplash, 2026](https://unsplash.com/photos/a-wooden-sauna-with-a-window-and-a-stack-of-rocks-nT8eHVXHw5o?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditShareLink) 

#### The German wellness market at a glance

- 85% of German travellers say experiencing nature is an important part of a successful holiday (CBI, 2025).
- 52% cite relaxation and escape from routine as one of their main motivations for travel.
- 36% consider having free time to relax an important factor when choosing a destination.

Structured, nature-based itineraries with measurable wellbeing benefits are particularly well-suited to this market. Popular long-haul destinations include Thailand, India, Sri Lanka, Bali, Costa Rica and Southern Africa.

Germany has one of Europe’s best-developed networks for wellness travel distribution. Specialist wellness tour operators play an important role, such as [FIT Reisen](http://www.fitreisen.de/), alongside mainstream tour operators that incorporate wellness products into broader holiday programmes. [ITB Berlin](https://www.itb.com/en) is one of the largest tourism events in Europe and a great way to meet buyers.

### France

France is Europe’s second-largest wellness tourism market. It recorded 41.5 million wellness tourism trips in 2024. It also generated $45.6 billion (USD) in wellness tourism expenditure, the highest among the selected European source markets. This reflects French wellness travellers’ high spending power. Wellness is well established in France through thermal spas, thalassotherapy, beauty treatments and preventative health. This means French consumers are very familiar with wellness products and services.

#### The French wellness market at a glance

- [78% of people take part](https://altiant.com/buzz-vs-reality-wellness-2024) in wellness activities as part of their weekly routine.
- 46% cite relaxation and escape from routine as one of their main motivations for travel (CBI, 2025).
- 28% consider having free time to relax an important factor when choosing a destination (CBI, 2025).
- 80% have spontaneously taken part in wellness activities while on holiday.
- 72% have taken a dedicated wellness holiday and would be interested in doing so again.
- The ideal length of a wellness holiday is [4–5 nights for 40% of travellers](https://altiant.com/buzz-vs-reality-wellness-2024), followed by 2–3 nights for 25%.
- [79% would be interested in taking a wellness holiday with a partner or spouse](https://altiant.com/buzz-vs-reality-wellness-2024), 31% with friends and 29% as a family.

French travellers look for high-quality, comfortable wellness experiences that combine relaxation with healthy food, local culture and nature. The French-speaking countries of Morocco, Tunisia and Mauritius are popular long-haul destinations, particularly for spa and coastal wellness holidays. Focus on what makes your offer distinctive. This means local healing traditions, exceptional cuisine and natural ingredients, rather than broad wellness claims.

France also has a well-developed distribution network. It has both specialist operators, such as [La Route des Sens](https://www.laroutedessens-pusignan.fr/), and premium companies, such as [Voyageurs du Monde](https://www.voyageursdumonde.fr/voyage-sur-mesure), which offers wellness holidays. [IFTM Top Resa](https://www.iftm.fr/en-gb.html) is the country’s leading travel trade event and an important opportunity to meet French buyers.

### United Kingdom

For many British travellers, holidays are an important way to relax, reduce stress and improve mental wellbeing. The UK generated 22.3 million wellness tourism trips and $19.1 billion (USD) in wellness tourism expenditure in 2024. This makes it one of Europe’s largest source markets for wellness travel. Around [80% of British consumers consider holidays important for their mental health](https://www.abta.com/industry-zone/reports-and-publications/abta-holiday-habits-reports/holiday-habits-2025-26). This reflects the growing role of travel in supporting healthier lifestyles.

#### The UK wellness market at a glance

- 50% cite relaxation and escape from routine as one of their main motivations for travel (CBI, 2025).
- 38% consider having free time to relax an important factor when choosing a destination (CBI, 2025).
- [69% of people take part in wellness activities](https://altiant.com/buzz-vs-reality-wellness-2024) as part of their weekly routine.
- 75% have spontaneously taken part in wellness activities while on holiday.
- 55% have taken a dedicated wellness holiday and would be interested in doing so again.
- The ideal length of a wellness holiday is 2–3 nights for 38% of travellers, followed by 4–5 nights for 31%.
- 84% would be interested in taking a wellness holiday with a partner or spouse, 47% with friends and 25% as a family.

Suppliers should highlight relaxation, mental wellbeing and experiences that fit easily into wider itineraries. Popular destinations include Costa Rica, Morocco, Bali, the Caribbean, South Africa and Peru.

Specialist operators are important distribution partners. They include [Healing Holidays](https://www.healingholidays.com/), [Wellbeing Escapes](https://www.wellbeingescapes.com/) and [The Healthy Holiday Company](https://thehealthyholidaycompany.co.uk/). [WTM London](https://www.wtm.com/london/en-gb.html) is an important event for connecting with UK buyers. Membership networks like the [Wellness Tourism Association](https://wellnesstourismassociation.org/) can help suppliers connect with wellness-focused tour operators, travel advisors, hotels and DMOs.

### Italy

In Italy, wellness is closely linked to everyday life through healthy food, outdoor living, thermal spas and the Mediterranean lifestyle. The country generated 11.5 million wellness tourism trips and $20.0 billion (USD) in wellness tourism expenditure in 2024. Italy is also one of the world’s 10 largest markets in 10 of the 11 wellness sectors measured by GWI. This shows the importance of wellbeing in Italian consumer culture.

Figure 8: Natural hot springs are popular in the Italian market

![Woman shown from behind, bathing in a natural hot spring](/sites/default/files/styles/image_medium/public/2026-09/STOCK_Figure%208%20-%20Natural%20hot%20springs%20are%20popular%20in%20the%20Italian%20market.jpg)

Source: [Joshua Sortino, Unsplash, 2026](https://unsplash.com/photos/woman-immerged-in-body-of-water-between-lands-under-cloudy-sky-utwkwDuGr1o?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditShareLink)

#### The Italian wellness market at a glance

- 43% cite relaxation and escape from routine as one of their main motivations for travel (CBI, 2025).
- 26% consider having free time to relax an important factor when choosing a destination (CBI, 2025).
- [22% of travellers take part in a wellness-related](https://www.enit.it/en/tourism-in-italy-enit-growth-in-wellness-travel) activity during their holiday.
- Spa experiences are the most popular wellness activity, accounting for 34%, followed by massages, thermal baths and beauty treatments.

Italian wellness culture is grounded in the quality of food, time spent outdoors and the rhythm of everyday Mediterranean life. Italian travellers do not primarily look for intensive health programmes. They want to experience a new quality of life. Lead with local cuisine, outdoor time and sense of place rather than resort-style spa packages.

Popular destinations include Peru, Colombia, Argentina, Mexico, Jordan and Cape Verde. Specialist operators feature wellness holidays, such as [SiVola Wellness Collection](http://www.sivola.it/). [TTG Travel Experience](https://www.ttgexpo.it/en) is Italy’s leading travel trade event.

### Spain

For Spanish travellers, wellness is often part of a broader holiday rather than the main reason for travelling. Spain generated 20.8 million wellness tourism trips and $16.7 billion (USD) in wellness tourism expenditure in 2024. Its culture of healthy eating, outdoor living and social wellbeing creates a natural affinity with wellness travel.

#### The Spanish wellness market at a glance

- 43% cite relaxation and escape from routine as one of their main motivations for travel (CBI, 2025).
- 27% consider having free time to relax an important factor when choosing a destination (CBI, 2025).
- Spain has one of Europe’s oldest populations, contributing to growing interest in healthy ageing and preventative wellbeing.
- Wellness is strongly associated with healthy lifestyles, Mediterranean food, outdoor activity and social wellbeing.
- Nature, outdoor recreation and relaxation are important components of wellness travel.

The growth in memberships from 67.7 million in 2023 to 71.6 million in 2024, was driven in part by large increases in the UK, which now has 11.5 million members (an increase of 6.1 per cent); Germany (11.7 million, up 3.6 per cent) and Spain (6.2 million an 8.7 per cent rise.)
